metadata.title: Collective teacher innovativeness in 48 countries: Effects of teacher autonomy, collaborative culture, and professional learning

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 teacher and principal public use files (TTGINT3 and TCGINTT3) covering 48 countries (Iceland excluded due to lack of public data). The analytic sample comprises 241,426 teachers nested in 15,672 schools, and the authors estimate a multilevel structural equation model (MSEM) in Mplus 8.3 with teacher- and school-level components. The manuscript does not report whether TALIS sampling weights or replicate weights were applied in the estimation, so the weighting strategy cannot be verified from the provided text. Because the analysis is model-based (MSEM with FIML for missingness) rather than ML prediction, the paper’s weighting transparency is limited; analysts using TALIS microdata should check the TALIS user guide for appropriate weight variables and whether Mplus was run with them.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The study does not use cognitive achievement plausible values (PVs); the dependent construct is a latent perception-based scale (Collective Teacher Innovativeness) and the mediator is a binary indicator of participation in professional learning activities. Missing data are handled via Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) in Mplus, which uses all available data under model-based assumptions rather than PV-based multiple imputation. The provided schema mapping treats FIML as multiple_imputation, but the paper’s approach is fundamentally likelihood-based estimation for missing responses within the SEM framework, not PV imputation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TALIS 2018 teacher public use file (TTGINT3) and principal public use file (TCGINTT3) with cross-sectional data collected between September 2017 and November 2018. The public use files contain data from 48 countries because Iceland has no public available data. The analytic model includes teachers nested in schools and estimates a doubly-latent contextual multilevel SEM; missing responses in model variables were handled with FIML. No additional country- or grade-specific subsampling is described in the provided text beyond the exclusion of Iceland and the use of the specified TALIS public use files.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel SEM fit: c2=20677.383 (df=190), CFI=0.99, RMSEA=0.02, SRMRw=0.01, SRMRb=0.04. Teacher-level paths: Collaborative Culture→Innovativeness b=0.433 (SE=0.005, p<.001); Teacher Autonomy→Innovativeness b=0.016 (SE=0.003, p<.001); Integrated Professional Learning→Innovativeness b=-0.011 (SE=0.002, p<.001). School-level paths: Collaborative Culture→Innovativeness b=0.641 (SE=0.011, p<.001); Teacher Autonomy→Innovativeness b=0.179 (SE=0.011, p<.001); Integrated Professional Learning→Innovativeness b=0.133 (SE=0.011, p<.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (teacher questionnaire; 48 countries) the study leveraged Collaborative Culture and Teacher Autonomy (plus teacher demographic controls) to model Collective Teacher Innovativeness, finding that Collaborative Culture had strong positive associations with innovativeness at both teacher and school levels, while Teacher Autonomy showed smaller positive effects at both levels. This indicates that strengthening collaborative, shared-decision school cultures may be a more powerful lever than classroom autonomy alone for promoting collective teacher innovativeness, though the study is cross-sectional and based on teachers’ perceptions.

main_findings.target_variable: Integrated Professional Learning (binary: formal + job-embedded participation)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Teacher-level path: Collaborative Culture→Integrated Professional Learning b=0.049 (SE=0.003, p<.001); Teacher Autonomy→Integrated Professional Learning b=0.004 (SE=0.003, p>.05). School-level paths: Collaborative Culture→Integrated Professional Learning b=0.348 (SE=0.013, p<.001); Teacher Autonomy→Integrated Professional Learning b=-0.027 (SE=0.014, p>.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (teacher questionnaire; 48 countries) the study leveraged Collaborative Culture and Teacher Autonomy to predict Integrated Professional Learning, finding that Collaborative Culture significantly increased the likelihood/extent of integrated professional learning at both teacher and school levels, whereas Teacher Autonomy had no significant association with integrated professional learning. This indicates that policies aiming to increase teachers’ participation in both formal and job-embedded learning should prioritize building collaborative school cultures rather than relying on classroom autonomy reforms alone.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data from 48 countries (241,426 teachers nested in 15,672 schools) to examine how teacher classroom autonomy and collaborative school culture relate to collective teacher innovativeness, and whether integrated professional learning mediates these relationships. The authors estimate a multilevel structural equation model in Mplus 8.3 and handle missingness using Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML), with model fit reported as c2=20677.383 (df=190), CFI=0.99, RMSEA=0.02, SRMRw=0.01, SRMRb=0.04. At the teacher level, Collaborative Culture strongly predicts innovativeness (b=0.433, p<.001) and Teacher Autonomy has a small positive effect (b=0.016, p<.001). At the school level, Collaborative Culture (b=0.641, p<.001) and Teacher Autonomy (b=0.179, p<.001) are both positive, while integrated professional learning is positive at the school level (b=0.133, p<.001) but negative at the teacher level (b=-0.011, p<.001). The mediation pattern is therefore mixed and the study is cross-sectional and perception-based, limiting causal interpretation.
